Get started with multimod

Source: vignettes/multimod.Rmd
multimod.Rmd

multimod represents a linear optimization model as an abstract syntax tree (AST) of sets, mappings, parameters, variables and equations, independent of any modeling language. This vignette takes one small model through the main operations: reading and translating, analyzing structure and redundancy, rendering to LaTeX, exporting, and solving. Each step is a single call on the same model object.

library(multimod)

A model

The package ships two example models. example_models$toy is a small capacity-expansion LP built with the constructors: three technologies supply two regions at least cost.

toy <- example_models$toy
toy
#> Model: toy
#> Description: two-region capacity expansion toy model
#> Language:  multimod 
#> Sets:  2 
#> Mappings:  2 
#> Aliases:  0 
#> Parameters:  4 
#> Variables:  3 
#> Equations:  3

Reading and translating

read_gmpl() reads a GNU MathProg model, with its data section, from a file or from text. The result is a multimod model of the same kind as toy.

src <- c(
  "set REGION;",
  "set TECH;",
  "param Demand{r in REGION};",
  "param Cost{t in TECH};",
  "var gen{t in TECH, r in REGION} >= 0;",
  "minimize total: sum{t in TECH, r in REGION} Cost[t] * gen[t,r];",
  "s.t. meet{r in REGION}: sum{t in TECH} gen[t,r] >= Demand[r];",
  "data;",
  "set REGION := north south;",
  "set TECH := coal wind;",
  "param Demand := north 10 south 5;",
  "param Cost := coal 3 wind 1;",
  "end;"
)
m <- read_gmpl(src)
m
#> Model: gmpl_model
#> Description: GMPL model from in-memory source
#> Source:  <in-memory> 
#> Language:  gmpl 
#> Sets:  2 
#> Mappings:  0 
#> Aliases:  2 
#> Parameters:  2 
#> Variables:  2 
#> Equations:  2

Any equation of the model renders to GAMS, JuMP and Pyomo:

meet <- m$equations$meet
cat(as_gams(meet))
#> meet[r]..
#>   sum(t, gen[t,r]) =g=
#>   Demand[r];
cat(as_jump(meet, model = m))
#> @constraint(
#>     model,
#>     meet[r in REGION],
#>     sum(gen[t, r] for t in TECH) >= get(Demand, r, DemandDef)
#> )
cat(as_pyomo(meet, model = m))
#> def _meet_rule(model, r):
#>     _expr = sum(model.gen[t, r] for t in model.TECH) >= model.Demand[r]
#>     if _expr is True or _expr is False:
#>         return Constraint.Feasible if _expr else Constraint.Infeasible
#>     return _expr
#> 
#> model.meet = Constraint(model.REGION, rule=_meet_rule)

read_gams() reads the linear subset of GAMS in the same way. A single equation can also be written as MathProg, GAMS or JuMP text with mm_equation(), which resolves its names against the model’s declarations:

cap <- mm_equation(
  toy,
  "eqCapTotal.. sum((tech, region), vCap(tech, region)) =l= 2000;",
  lang = "gams"
)
cat(as_gmpl(cap, model = toy))
#> s.t. eqCapTotal: sum{t in tech, r in region}(vCap[t,r]) <= 2000;

Structure and redundancy

validate() checks that every symbol an equation refers to is declared and that the dimensions agree. model_to_lp() assembles the constraint matrix, and check_matrix_numbers() reports the range of its coefficients, which indicates how well scaled the problem is for a solver.

validate(toy)
#> Model Validation Results
#> ========================
#> 
#> Status: VALID ✓
#> 
#> INFO:
#>   ℹ Objective function: minimize vCost 
#>   ℹ Found 2 index_aliases covering 2 sets/aliases
lp <- model_to_lp(toy)
dim(lp$A)
#> [1]  9 13
chk <- check_matrix_numbers(lp, verbose = FALSE)
chk$summary[, c("section", "entries", "min_abs", "max_abs", "orders")]
#>     section entries min_abs max_abs orders
#> 1   COLUMNS      29    0.25     120    2.7
#> 2 OBJECTIVE       1    1.00       1    0.0
#> 3       RHS      10  600.00    1000    0.2
#> 4    BOUNDS       0      NA      NA     NA

Redundancy is easier to see on a larger model. example_models$energyRt holds the energyRt energy system model, parsed from its GAMS source with data attached. analyze_parameter_redundancy() measures how many of each parameter’s values repeat across a dimension, which is what folding removes, and trim_model() marks the symbols that the data leaves unused:

big <- example_models$energyRt$multimod
red <- analyze_parameter_redundancy(big, verbose = FALSE)
head(red[order(-red$orig_redundancy_pct),
         c("param_name", "orig_rows", "orig_unique", "orig_redundancy_pct")])
#>        param_name orig_rows orig_unique orig_redundancy_pct
#> 3   pTechCinp2use      1344           3                99.8
#> 30    pTradeIrEff       576           1                99.8
#> 8       pTechAfLo       336           1                99.7
#> 23 pStorageInpEff       336           1                99.7
#> 24 pStorageOutEff       336           1                99.7
#> 20  pTimesliceAgg       180           1                99.4

trimmed <- trim_model(big, verbose = FALSE)
get_trim_summary(trimmed, format = "data.frame")
#>   element_type total trimmed remaining percent_trimmed
#> 1         sets    27       6        21            22.2
#> 2   parameters   218       1       217             0.5
#> 3     mappings   324     160       164            49.4
#> 4    variables    93      10        83            10.8
#> 5    equations   153     103        50            67.3

The “Folding and trimming” article on the website applies both reductions and shows that the optimum is unchanged.

LaTeX

as_latex() renders any node as LaTeX math, and write_latex() writes the whole model as a LaTeX document. The demand balance of toy:

eq <- toy$equations$eqDemand
lhs <- as_latex(eq$lhs)
rhs <- as_latex(eq$rhs)
lhs
#> [1] "\\sum_{\\texttt{tech}} \\bm{\\mathit{vGen}}_{\\texttt{tech},\\texttt{region}}"

∑𝚝𝚎𝚌𝚑𝑣𝐺𝑒𝑛𝚝𝚎𝚌𝚑,𝚛𝚎𝚐𝚒𝚘𝚗≥𝗉𝖣𝖾𝗆𝖺𝗇𝖽𝚛𝚎𝚐𝚒𝚘𝚗 \sum_{\texttt{tech}} \boldsymbol{\mathit{vGen}}_{\texttt{tech},\texttt{region}} \ge \mathsf{pDemand}_{\texttt{region}}

Exporting

write_gmpl(), write_jump(), write_pyomo() and write_gams() render the whole model in one language. Without a file they return the code; the declarations, objective and constraints of toy in MathProg:

code <- write_gmpl(toy)
cat(code[13:27], sep = "\n")
#> param pCapCost{tech};  # annualized capacity cost, EUR/kW
#> param pVarCost{tech};  # variable cost, EUR/MWh
#> param pAvail{tech,region};  # availability factor
#> param pDemand{region};  # annual demand, MWh
#> 
#> var vCap{t in tech, r in region} >= 0;  # installed capacity, kW
#> var vGen{t in tech, r in region} >= 0;  # generation, MWh
#> 
#> minimize vCost: sum{t in tech, r in region} (pCapCost[t] * vCap[t,r] + pVarCost[t] * vGen[t,r]);
#> 
#> # generation is limited by available capacity
#> s.t. eqCapLim{(h,r) in mTR}: vGen[h,r] <= pAvail[h,r] * vCap[h,r];
#> 
#> # demand is met in every region
#> s.t. eqDemand{r in mR}: sum{t in tech} vGen[t,r] >= pDemand[r];

save_model() stores the model and its data as a workspace of CSV, Arrow IPC or Parquet files, which the generated JuMP and Pyomo code reads at run time. model_to_json() serializes the structure for other tools.

ws <- tempfile("toy-")
toy <- save_model(toy, ws, format = "csv", verbose = FALSE)
list.files(ws, recursive = TRUE)
#>  [1] "format.txt"                   "mappings/mappings.csv"       
#>  [3] "mappings/mR/data.csv"         "mappings/mTR/data.csv"       
#>  [5] "metadata.json"                "model.rds"                   
#>  [7] "parameters/parameters.csv"    "parameters/pAvail/data.csv"  
#>  [9] "parameters/pCapCost/data.csv" "parameters/pDemand/data.csv" 
#> [11] "parameters/pVarCost/data.csv" "sets/region/data.csv"        
#> [13] "sets/sets.csv"                "sets/tech/data.csv"

json <- model_to_json(toy)
substr(json, 1, 120)
#> [1] "{\n  \"multimod_schema\": \"1.0\",\n  \"node\": \"model\",\n  \"data_inlined\": false,\n  \"name\": \"toy\",\n  \"desc\": \"two-region capacit"

Solving

solve_highs() assembles the LP and solves it in R with the ‘highs’ package:

result <- solve_highs(toy, attach = FALSE)
result$objective
#> [1] 198000

solve_gmpl(), solve_jump() and solve_pyomo() solve the generated code with GLPK, Julia or Python instead, and load the solution back into the model.
